title: Health Consequences of Female Genital Mutilation

headings.title: Introduction to Female Genital Mutilation and Classification
headings.content: Female Genital Mutilation (FGM) encompasses all procedures involving partial or total removal of the external female genitalia or other injury to the female genital organs for non-medical reasons. Internationally recognized and classified by the World Health Organization into four distinct types, FGM is a deeply entrenched harmful traditional practice violating fundamental human rights and health. Type I, often referred to as clitoridectomy, involves the partial or total removal of the clitoris and/or the prepuce. Type II, or excision, entails the partial or total removal of the clitoris and the labia minora, with or without excision of the labia majora. Type III, the most severe form, is infibulation; this involves narrowing of the vaginal orifice through the creation of a covering seal by cutting and repositioning the labia minora or majora, with or without excision of the clitoris. Type IV includes all other harmful procedures to the female genitalia for non-medical purposes, such as pricking, piercing, incising, scraping, and cauterization. For nursing students in Nigeria, understanding these classifications is crucial for accurate clinical documentation, holistic care planning, and implementing culturally sensitive community health education aimed at eradication.

headings.title: Immediate Physical and Surgical Complications
headings.content: The immediate physical and surgical complications of FGM occur during or shortly after the procedure is performed. Because these procedures are frequently carried out in non-sterile community settings by traditional practitioners using crude instruments like unsterilized razor blades, knives, or pieces of glass without anesthesia, the physiological toll is immense. Severe pain is an immediate universal consequence, which can induce neurogenic shock. Hemorrhage is another critical acute risk, often leading to severe anemia, hypovolemic shock, and even death if prompt medical intervention is not secured. Localized and systemic infections, including tetanus, sepsis, and gangrene, frequently develop due to the introduction of pathogens into open wounds. Accidental injury to adjacent anatomical structures such as the urethra, bladder, rectum, and perineum is common during the cutting process. Acute urinary retention can also occur secondary to swelling, pain, and fear of passing urine over raw wounds. For Nigerian nurses working in emergency departments and primary health care centers, recognizing these immediate surgical complications is vital for delivering life-saving triage, resuscitation, and stabilization.

headings.title: Long-Term Urological and Gynecological Sequelae
headings.content: Long-term urological and gynecological sequelae persist for years or even a lifetime after the initial FGM procedure. Scar tissue formation, keloid development, and labial adhesions are widespread, causing chronic physical discomfort and anatomical distortion. Urological complications stem from obstruction and scarring around the urethral meatus, leading to recurrent urinary tract infections (UTIs), dysuria, chronic pelvic discomfort, and the formation of calculi in the bladder or urethra. Gynecological sequelae include chronic vulvar pain, dysmenorrhea caused by obstructed menstrual flow (hematocolpos) due to tight scar tissue or infibulation seals, and chronic vaginal discharge. Furthermore, the entrapment of nerve endings within scar tissue can produce persistent neuropathic pain and hypersensitivity. Women with Type III infibulation often require defibulation to relieve trapped menstrual blood and urine, only to face ongoing structural vulnerability. Nurses in gynecological clinics must be equipped to diagnose these chronic sequelae, offer empathetic support, and coordinate specialized surgical referrals when necessary.

headings.title: Obstetric Complications and Risks During Childbirth
headings.content: Obstetric complications and risks during childbirth are significantly elevated among women who have undergone FGM, particularly Types II and III. The presence of rigid scar tissue, fibrosis, and narrowed vaginal openings reduces the elasticity of the birth canal, often necessitating prolonged and obstructed labor. This increases the likelihood of perineal tears, obstetric fistula formation (vesicovaginal or rectovaginal), and uterine rupture. Fetal distress and intrauterine hypoxia are common due to prolonged second-stage labor, which substantially elevates neonatal morbidity and perinatal mortality rates. Additionally, women with FGM frequently require episiotomies, yet healthcare providers may struggle to perform adequate deliveries or surgical repairs due to distorted anatomy. Postpartum hemorrhage is another critical risk, driven by uterine atony from prolonged labor or extensive tissue lacerations. For midwives and obstetric nurses practicing in Nigeria, understanding these intrapartum risks is essential for vigilant monitoring, timely surgical intervention (such as anterior episiotomy or caesarean section), and ensuring safe delivery outcomes.

headings.title: Psychological, Emotional, and Sexual Health Impacts
headings.content: Beyond the physical morbidity, FGM profoundly impacts the psychological, emotional, and sexual well-being of affected women and girls. The experience of the trauma—often inflicted during childhood under betrayal of trust by caregivers—frequently leads to post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), chronic anxiety, depression, low self-esteem, and severe phobias related to medical and gynecological examinations. Psychosomatic symptoms, sleep disturbances, and feelings of incompleteness or betrayal are also widely reported. From a sexual health perspective, the removal of or damage to highly sensitive erogenous zones like the clitoris, combined with vaginal narrowing and scarring, leads to dyspareunia (painful intercourse), reduced or absent sexual desire, difficulty or inability to achieve orgasm, and profound psychological aversion to sexual intimacy. This can strain marital relationships and contribute to domestic friction or social isolation. Nurses must approach patients with sensitivity, utilizing trauma-informed care principles to validate these emotional and sexual challenges without judgment.

headings.title: Nursing Assessment and Clinical Identification
headings.content: Nursing assessment and clinical identification of FGM require a high index of suspicion, cultural sensitivity, and exceptional clinical communication skills. Many women and girls may conceal their status due to cultural taboos, fear of stigma, or shame. Nurses must conduct comprehensive physical assessments during routine health checks, antenatal visits, or gynecological examinations while maintaining strict privacy and confidentiality. Assessment should include taking a detailed obstetric and gynecological history, noting any signs of scarring, anatomical asymmetry, or altered genitalia. Nurses should look for clinical indicators such as chronic urinary symptoms, painful menstruation, or unexplained difficulties during pelvic exams. It is imperative that nurses use non-judgmental language, build a trusting therapeutic nurse-patient relationship, and ensure informed consent before any physical inspection. Documenting findings accurately is essential for continuity of care and legal protection, while also providing an opportunity to offer supportive counseling and gentle referral pathways for specialized psychological or surgical management.

headings.title: Holistic Management and Patient Care Strategies
headings.content: Holistic management and patient care strategies for FGM survivors demand an interdisciplinary approach that addresses physical, psychological, and social health dimensions. Clinical care includes pain management for chronic pelvic pain, surgical interventions such as defibulation (or de-infibulation) for infibulated women prior to childbirth or to relieve urinary and menstrual obstructions, and reconstructive counseling. Psychological support must involve trauma-informed counseling, cognitive behavioral therapy, and support groups to help survivors process past trauma, alleviate anxiety, and navigate sexual health concerns. In obstetric settings, holistic care requires specialized intrapartum monitoring, gentle handling, avoidance of routine restrictive episiotomies where possible, and coordinated multidisciplinary teamwork involving obstetricians, midwives, mental health professionals, and social workers. For Nigerian nurses, acting as a patient advocate, educator, and compassionate caregiver ensures that survivors receive comprehensive care that respects their dignity and promotes long-term healing and well-being.

headings.title: Prevention, Advocacy, and the Role of the Nurse in Nigeria
headings.content: Prevention, advocacy, and the role of the nurse in Nigeria are critical in the national campaign to abandon FGM. Nurses occupy a frontline position in communities, primary healthcare clinics, and tertiary hospitals, making them pivotal agents of social and behavioral change. Prevention strategies include community mobilization, engaging traditional and religious leaders, educating parents and youth on the health hazards of FGM, and promoting girl-child education and empowerment. Nurses must actively participate in advocacy by supporting legislative frameworks, such as the Violence Against Persons Prohibition (VAPP) Act, which criminalizes FGM in many Nigerian states. Furthermore, nurses must integrate health education into routine antenatal, postnatal, and immunization clinics to debunk myths surrounding FGM, such as beliefs regarding hygiene, chastity, or enhanced fertility. By fostering open dialogues, providing compassionate care, and collaborating with non-governmental organizations and public health agencies, Nigerian nurses contribute significantly to creating a future free from the scourge of female genital mutilation.
